name: Alligation
seoDesc: Alligation: work out lower concentration from the higher concentration and the required concentration. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Give the Alligation calculator the higher concentration, the required concentration, the higher concentration volume and the lower concentration volume and it returns lower concentration. That makes it useful for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Alligation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Alligation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports lower concentration in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the higher concentration, the required concentration, the higher concentration volume and the lower concentration volume.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Alligation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Lower concentration=(higher concentration × lower concentration volume − higher concentration × required concentration volume + required concentration volume × required concentration) ÷ lower concentration volume
Lower concentration=(higher concentration volume × higher concentration − required concentration volume × required concentration) ÷ (higher concentration volume − required concentration volume)
Mult value=(higher concentration, lower concentration, required concentration)
Hi con=((-lower concentration + required concentration) × (higher concentration, lower concentration, required concentration))
Low con=((higher concentration − required concentration) × (higher concentration, lower concentration, required concentration))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Higher concentration = 10, Required concentration = 10, Lower concentration volume = 10 mL and Required concentration volume = 10 mL. The calculator returns Lower concentration = 10.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Lower concentration = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Higher concentration = 10 and Required concentration = 10.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Volume, opening in milliliters
  • Volume, opening in milliliters
  • Volume, opening in milliliters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Alligation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the higher concentration, the required concentration and the higher concentration volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Alligation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns lower concentration, derived from the higher concentration, the required concentration and the higher concentration volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Alligation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the higher concentration, the required concentration, the higher concentration volume and the lower concentration volume, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter higher concentration volume in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Higher concentration volume opens in milliliters and the chip beside it offers 40 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Lower concentration = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Alligation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
